o: We may pay ±1 per unit to change any element; minimize total cost to make the array monotone (either direction). Example 1 pays 4 to become [3,3,3,3,0]. Checking monotonicity first handles Examples 2–3 with cost 0. The classic tool is the 'slope trick' / max-heap technique: processing left to right for non-decreasing order, whenever the running maximum exceeds the current element, we conceptually lower earlier peaks to the current value, charging the difference, and push the current value as the new peak. Doing this for both directions and taking the minimum gives the answer.
k: For non-decreasing: sweep with a max-heap of 'peaks'; when the current value x is smaller than the peak p, pay p−x, pop p, and push x — this optimally merges the violation.
Run the same procedure on the reversed array to get the non-increasing cost; answer is the min of the two.
Alternatively, an O(n · V) DP over final values with prefix-min transitions works given small value bounds.

a.i: Maintain a max-heap representing possible final values of the processed prefix. When x < heap top p, the cheapest fix lowers that peak to x, costing p − x; replacing p with x keeps the heap a valid set of candidate levels. Summing these costs yields the minimal cost for a non-decreasing arrangement.
s: For each x in a: push -x; if -heap.top() > x, add (-heap.top() - x) to total, pop and push -x.
a.t: O(n log n) — each element causes O(log n) heap work, run twice.

a.i: dp[i][v] = minimum cost so that the first i+1 elements form a non-decreasing sequence ending at value v. Transition: dp[i][v] = |nums[i] − v| + min(dp[i-1][u]) for u ≤ v, computed with a running prefix minimum. Run it forward (non-decreasing) and backward (non-increasing) and take the smaller answer. With n, V ≤ 1000 this is about 10^6 operations.
s: Let M = max(nums). Initialize dp[v] = |nums[0] − v| for v in 0..M.
For each subsequent x: keep running best = min(dp[0..v]), set ndp[v] = best + |x − v|.
Answer = min(min(dp) forward, min(dp) on reversed array).
a.t: O(n · V) where V = max(nums) — each of n steps scans V candidate values.

w: In an interview, lead with the heap method (it meets the O(n log n) follow-up); the DP is easier to prove correct and fine for these constraints. Pitfall: forgetting to also solve the non-increasing direction — the answer is the MINIMUM of the two, not just non-decreasing. Costs fit in 64-bit (up to ~10^9). Follow-up: reconstruct an actual optimal array — store parent pointers in the DP or track heap levels in slope trick.
